items.gist: The passage maps the mālinī garland of phonemes onto bodily locations from crown to feet. It establishes the phonematic nyāsa as a bodily placement of the alphabet.
The śāktī body arises from mutual agitation of bīja and yoni, yet the nādi-to-pha order remains the principal sequence. It affirms both emanative mixture and ordered phonematic primacy.
The full speech-power is gathered and named mālinī, mother-like because it will become. It is the garland of Rudras and bearer of siddhi and liberation.
Mālinī is fruitful, worshipful, and endowed with powers of dissolution and bestowal. Each phoneme is full because of its Śiva-śakti nature.
Mantras placed by nyāsa are completed by mālinī when rite is deficient. The distinction of yoni is specified for the purpose of the rite.
Even mantras such as gāruḍa are perfected by mālinī for siddhi. For liberation, however, power alone suffices without such completion.
One may nyāsa mātṛkā or mālinī in order or simultaneously. The two piṇḍas akṣahrīṃ and naphahrīṃ are named for the two modes.
Nyāsa may be done with one or both piṇḍas, collectively or separately. The placements may be ordered or unordered, then combined.
One seeking siddhi performs more rite, while one seeking liberation may act as desired. The purpose of all nyāsa and related acts is Śiva-tāpatti.
After nyāsa, one proceeds to worship in the argha vessel with the placed deities. All agents are shown non-different from Śiva in worship.
Just as a trained horse does not exceed its training, agents habituated by worship lose duality. For one established in unity, the universe suddenly shines as full Śiva.
The guru praises Śiva-worship as a sweet festival. Those who worship for full Śiva-entry are themselves Śiva, so what further fruit is needed?
Through unity-samāpatti, the rite gives supreme fruit and mantra-unity. Parameśvara says success comes by remembrance alone, not by rule or sequence.
The rite gives identity of all agents with Śiva through nyāsa. The argha vessel is the recipient, and its contents are instruments of purification and worship.
Everything touched by argha-vessel water is purified. No un-purified thing should be used, and impurity is understood from paśu-conditioning.
Purity may come from prior state or supplied means. Fitness and unfitness are declared according to proximity to consciousness and grace.
For vīras, gurus immerse consciousness in the rite. Bliss arising from immersion makes the rite fit for worship.
In kula practice, substances such as wine have supreme power. Rules such as pañcagavya purity, avabhṛtha bath, and wife's presence are mentioned.
Śaiva practice overrides Vedic prohibitions in its own sphere. The one who knows Śiva-nondifference triumphs over smārta rules.
Munis' words can uproot Vedic authority, and Vedic prohibitions may be declared permissible. Thus Śiva's word is not obstructed by śruti in its proper sphere.
Having discussed these matters, the text returns to the rite. After nyāsa and purification of all implements, one performs external worship.
